query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small tungsten addition into a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high‐entropy alloy will promote the formation of coherent tungsten‐rich nano-precipitates that impede dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding, thereby enhancing elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance compared to the tungsten-free alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as the primary constituents and at least three additional elements each present in the 5–35 at% range, exhibiting a largely homogeneous, as-cast or solution-treated microstructure.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a minor tungsten content into the alloy formulation.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., tensile and/or creep tests) conducted within the temperature range typical for high-temperature applications (approximately 600–1000°C) under thermal-mechanical loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of finely dispersed, coherent tungsten-rich nano-precipitates within the alloy matrix.
generation.mechanism: The tungsten addition facilitates precipitation strengthening by promoting the nucleation of tungsten-rich precipitates, which serve as obstacles to dislocation glide and grain-boundary sliding, thereby enhancing yield strength and reducing creep rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-doped alloy is expected to show improved elevated-temperature mechanical properties, with higher yield strength and enhanced creep resistance relative to an otherwise identical alloy without tungsten.
generation.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without any tungsten addition.
generation.boundary: The intervention applies to alloy compositions satisfying high-entropy criteria (each element between 5–35 at%) and testing conditions where elevated-temperature phases are stable (roughly 600–1000°C); care must be taken to avoid processing conditions that lead to unwanted phase separation.
generation.uncertainty: While an improvement is anticipated based on precipitation-strengthening mechanisms, the precise magnitude of the enhancement remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from the same titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy batch: one with a small tungsten addition and one control without tungsten. Process both sets under identical conditions to obtain comparable microstructures. Conduct high-temperature tensile and/or creep tests within the 600–1000°C range, and perform microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM, XRD) to assess the presence, distribution, and coherence of tungsten-rich nano-precipitates.
measurements: Creep strain rate under constant load
Precipitate identification and characterization (size, distribution, and coherence)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in yield strength and/or a reduction in creep rate compared to the control, or if the anticipated coherent tungsten-rich precipitates are not detected via microstructural analysis, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a small refractory element (e.g., ~5 at% tungsten) followed by an aging heat treatment will promote the formation of coherent tungsten-rich precipitates that impede dislocation motion and slow creep, thereby improving the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy compared with an untreated alloy.
drafts.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy (with at least five elements at 5–35 at% each) in a homogeneous, as-cast or solution-treated condition where Ti and Ni dominate.
drafts.intervention: Incorporate approximately 5 at% tungsten into the alloy composition and apply an aging heat treatment (for example, around 700°C for 4 hours) to foster precipitate development.
drafts.conditions: The alloy is evaluated under elevated-temperature conditions (e.g., 600–800°C) relevant to high-temperature mechanical applications. The overall composition must remain within high-entropy limits (each element between 5 and 35 at%).
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of finely dispersed, coherent tungsten-rich precipitates within the primary matrix.
drafts.mechanism: The tungsten-rich precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion, reducing creep and enhancing yield strength at high temperatures. This precipitation strengthening mechanism is expected to delay dislocation glide and climb especially under prolonged thermal exposure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-modified and aged alloy will exhibit a measurable improvement in elevated-temperature properties, such as increased creep resistance and higher yield strength (for example, on the order of a 15–25% improvement) relative to a control alloy without tungsten addition and aging.
drafts.baseline: The performance of the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy in its native, untreated condition (no tungsten addition and no aging treatment) under equivalent high-temperature mechanical testing.
drafts.boundary: This intervention applies provided the overall composition remains within the standard high-entropy alloy limits (5–35 at% per element) and that the aging treatment is performed within the 600–800°C temperature range. Significant deviations in tungsten content or heat treatment parameters may alter the expected precipitate formation and the strengthening effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy specimens: one set with an additional ~5 at% tungsten and subjected to an aging heat treatment at ~700°C for 4 hours, and a control set without tungsten addition or aging treatment. Conduct high-temperature tensile and creep tests at a chosen elevated temperature (e.g., 700°C) and perform microstructural analysis (using TEM/SEM) to verify precipitate formation.
measurements: Creep rate under a constant load
High-temperature yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Characterization of precipitate size, distribution, and coherency via TEM/SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-added and aged alloy does not exhibit at least a 15% improvement in high-temperature mechanical properties (i.e., yield strength or creep resistance) compared to the control, or if coherent tungsten-rich precipitates are not observed in the microstructural analysis, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A controlled aging treatment that promotes the in situ formation of coherent Ni3Ti precipitates in a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will enhance its elevated-temperature creep resistance compared to its as-cast state.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy designed with titanium and nickel as primary constituents and three or more additional elements each present at 5–35 at% to satisfy the high-entropy criterion.
drafts.intervention: Apply a heat treatment (aging) regime at approximately 800°C for 2 hours followed by controlled cooling to encourage the nucleation and growth of Ni3Ti precipitates.
drafts.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical testing conducted at around 750°C under constant load conditions, within the stability range of the Ni3Ti phase.
drafts.structural_mediator: The in situ formation of coherent Ni3Ti intermetallic precipitates evenly distributed in the alloy matrix.
drafts.mechanism: The Ni3Ti precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding, thereby impeding creep deformation and enhancing mechanical strength at high temperatures.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The aged alloy will exhibit a lower steady-state creep rate and higher yield strength at elevated temperatures (e.g., a 20% or greater improvement) relative to the as-cast alloy.
drafts.baseline: The as-cast state of the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy with the same overall composition but without any post-casting heat treatment.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable over compositions in which Ti and Ni are primary constituents with all additional elements within the 5–35 at% range and for elevated-temperature service conditions between approximately 600°C and 800°C, where the Ni3Ti phase is thermally stable.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy batch. Subject one set to the specified aging treatment (800°C for 2 hours with controlled cooling) and retain the other set as-cast. Conduct elevated-temperature creep tests at 750°C under identical constant load conditions. Characterize the microstructure of both sets using TEM and SEM to assess the presence, size, and distribution of Ni3Ti precipitates.
measurements: Creep rate during high-temperature constant load testing
Microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM) quantifying precipitate fraction and morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than 20% enhancement in creep resistance or yield strength) compared to the as-cast samples, or if the anticipated coherent Ni3Ti precipitates are not observed in the microstructural analysis, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A post‐processing homogenization aging treatment that promotes the in situ formation of coherent B2-type precipitates will increase the elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance of a titanium–nickel primary high‐entropy alloy compared to its as-cast state.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as the primary constituents (each within 5–35 at%) along with at least three additional elements to satisfy the composition criteria, initially exhibiting a largely random solid-solution microstructure.
drafts.intervention: Apply a tailored homogenization aging heat treatment (i.e. hold at an intermediate elevated temperature for a specific time period) to induce controlled precipitation of a coherent B2 ordered phase.
drafts.conditions: Heat treatment parameters (temperature, time, and cooling rate) must be chosen within the phase stability range of the alloy to ensure precipitate formation without causing deleterious phase separation; subsequent mechanical testing should be performed at temperatures comparable to service conditions (e.g., 650–800°C). The overall elemental compositions must remain within 5–35 at% per element.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation and distribution of nanoscale coherent B2 precipitates at grain boundaries and within grains
drafts.mechanism: The induced coherent B2 precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperatures, thereby enhancing yield strength and creep resistance through precipitation-strengthening mechanisms.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast alloy, the heat-treated alloy is predicted to exhibit higher yield strength and longer creep rupture life under elevated-temperature testing; the improvement is expected in a manner that is quantifiable (e.g., an increase in yield strength by a significant margin relative to baseline), though the precise magnitude remains uncertain.
drafts.baseline: The as-cast titanium–nickel primary high-entropy alloy displaying a random solid-solution microstructure without engineered precipitates.
drafts.boundary: The intervention is limited to alloys that satisfy high-entropy criteria (each element between 5–35 at%) and to heat-treatment conditions that avoid melting, unwanted secondary phases, or coarse precipitate formation which could deteriorate mechanical properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the titanium–nickel primary high-entropy alloy: one set processed by the proposed homogenization aging treatment and a control set kept in the as-cast state. Subject both sets to identical elevated-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests and creep rupture experiments at 650–800°C). Microstructural analysis using techniques such as transmission electron microscopy (TEM) should be performed to confirm the presence or absence of coherent B2 precipitates.
measurements: Precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated alloy does not display a statistically significant improvement in elevated-temperature mechanical properties (yield strength and creep resistance), or if microstructural analysis fails to confirm the formation of coherent B2 precipitates compared to the as-cast sample, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a minor tungsten (W) content (2–3 at%) to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will promote the formation of coherent tungsten-rich nano-precipitates that impede dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding, thereby enhancing elevated-temperature strength and creep resistance relative to the tungsten-free alloy.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as primary constituents and additional elements each in the 5–35 at% range.
drafts.intervention: Introduce 2–3 at% tungsten into the alloy formulation.
drafts.conditions: Elevated temperatures (approximately 800–1000°C) under thermal-mechanical loading conditions (e.g., tensile and creep tests).
drafts.structural_mediator: Coherent tungsten-rich nano-precipitates that form within the grain interiors and/or along grain boundaries.
drafts.mechanism: The tungsten addition facilitates precipitation strengthening by forming stable, coherent nano-scale precipitates that obstruct dislocation movement and inhibit grain-boundary sliding, thereby enhancing strength and creep resistance at high temperatures.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-doped alloy will exhibit higher yield strength and improved creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the similar alloy without tungsten, along with clear evidence of tungsten-rich precipitate formation in microstructural analyses.
drafts.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without tungsten addition.
drafts.boundary: The alloy composition must remain within the high-entropy regime (each element in the 5–35 at% range) and the testing must be conducted at temperatures up to ~1000°C; care must be taken to avoid processing conditions that could lead to formation of unwanted secondary phases.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the titanium-nickel primary high-entropy alloy: one as the baseline and one with an added 2–3 at% tungsten. Process both batches under similar conditions to ensure comparable microstructures. Subject samples from both batches to tensile and creep tests at 800–1000°C. Additionally, perform microstructural characterization (e.g., transmission electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction) to identify and quantify the presence, size, and coherence of tungsten-rich precipitates.
measurements: Identification and quantification of nano-precipitates (size, distribution, coherence)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-doped alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (e.g., a measurable increase in yield strength and reduction in creep rate by a predetermined threshold) over the baseline, or if microstructural analysis does not reveal tungsten-rich nano-precipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.
